title: Holy Roman Shorthand
bodyHtml:
Before the printing press was invented, books had to be copied by hand. In Medieval Europe, most of this copying was done by monks. Poor lighting and other factors made this a difficult, often painful, task1 – so it’s no wonder that monks developed an extensive system of abbreviations to speed up their work!

For example, if a monk wanted to write the Latin words revertitur and illorum, they might have written:

Below are some examples of abbreviated Latin2 words you might find in a Medieval manuscript. Note that we’ve made some formatting changes when typing them up. Next to each one is the full (un-shortened) Latin word it corresponds to. In the right column, one possible English translation of the word is given. The English translations, and knowledge of Latin in general, aren’t necessary or helpful to solve this problem.

A1. Fill in the blanks (a) to (f) with the number (1–6) of the correct abbreviation from the list below:

1. fotis    2. ītoductū    3. 9u9sao    4. 9pxio    5. cau97    6. matis

A2. There can be many ways to abbreviate a Latin word. Below are 5 abbreviated words. 4 of them stand for the same Latin word. Write the letter of the one that does not match the others.

a. 9probatum    b. cōprobatū    c. compobatum    d. 9probat9    e. 9probatū

In English, we sometimes use the symbol & as an abbreviation for and. This symbol originally comes from the Latin word et, meaning “and”. In some fonts, the way that this symbol is written makes it easier to see how it came from the letter e plus the letter t. Here is one example:

A3. Some monks used the symbol & in their writing in the same contexts where one of the symbols listed below might be used. Which one?

a. 7    b. 9    c. ī    d. ō    e. ū

A4. Give abbreviated forms for the Latin words in the table below, labeled (a) through (f). You should write your abbreviations using the numerical codes shown in the symbol bank, writing one number from 1 to 22 for each symbol. Notes:

  • Some symbols appear multiple times in the symbol bank, always with the same number. You should use a given symbol no more times than it appears in the symbol bank. For example, there are four copies of n (number 9), so you should not use the number 9 more than four times in your answers.
  • As A2 showed, there can be more than one way to abbreviate a Latin word. However, for this question (A4), there is only one correct abbreviation for each Latin word, because other ways of abbreviating would not satisfy the constraints imposed by the symbol bank.
  • Some symbols will be left over in the symbol bank after you complete A4—see A5 for more details.

For example, if you thought the answer to (a) was d9, your answer would be 3 22, with 3 standing for d and 22 standing for 9.

A5. If you have completed A4 correctly, there should be six numbers left over in the symbol bank. The symbols corresponding to these numbers can be arranged into an English word that could be a good birthday gift for a Medieval monk. What is the English word?

  1. A quote from the 10th century about manuscript copying reads: “It dims your eyes, makes your back ache, and knits your chest and belly together. It is a terrible ordeal for the whole body.”
  2. Latin was the language of ancient Rome. In Medieval Europe, Latin continued to be used in many contexts, such as in religious and scholarly settings.

questions.partPrompt: Fill in the blanks (a) to (f) with the number (1–6) of the correct abbreviation: 1. fᵒtis  2. ītᵒductū  3. 9u⁹saᵒ  4. 9pˣio  5. cau⁹7  6. mᵃtis

hints.text: Line each abbreviated word up letter by letter with its full Latin word. Every plain letter matches; wherever a strange sign appears, some letters of the full word have gone missing. Write down which letters each sign is 'covering'. (Remember that in Latin manuscripts u and v are the same letter.)

There are two different kinds of shortcut. (1) A bar (macron) written over a vowel stands for that vowel plus a following m or n — and a bar can cover more than one letter. (2) A superscript or special sign stands for a whole chunk of missing letters: some superscript letters mark that letters right around them (very often an r) were dropped, while the number-like signs 7, 9, superscript 9 and superscript 2 each stand for a fixed group of letters. For A4, treat the symbol bank as a jigsaw: if a letter you need (such as plain r) is not in the bank at all, you are forced to use a shortcut sign there.

Work through a given example. In ꝑcul = procul, everything after the first sign (c-u-l) already matches the end of procul, so the single sign ꝑ must be doing the work of 'pro' — expect that same sign wherever 'pro' shows up. Similarly, in illoꝛ = illorum, 'illo' matches, so the final crossed sign spells 'rum'.

explanationHtml:
What kind of puzzle is this?

Medieval scribes saved time (and ink, and parchment) by leaving letters out and marking the gap with a special sign. Our job is to work out the value of each sign by comparing the short form with the full Latin word. Two facts about medieval Latin writing help: u and v are the same letter, and a bar (called a macron) over a letter means “an m or n was left out here.”

Step 1: decode the five given examples

  • ꝑcul = procul. The letters c-u-l already match, so ꝑ alone = pro.
  • illoꝝ = illorum. illo matches, so the crossed sign ꝝ = rum.
  • su9 = suus. su matches, so superscript 9 = us at the end of a word.
  • reu9ti2 = revertitur. Read it as re-u(=v)-9-ti-2: re + v + ? + ti + ? must give re-v-er-ti-ur. So the same superscript 9 can also stand for er, and superscript 2 = ur.
  • īp9p7uu = imperpetuum. Piece by piece: ī = im (bar = missing m), p9 = per, then p7 = pet, so 7 = et; finally the bar over uu gives uum.

The other kind of sign is a superscript letter. It marks that letters next to it were dropped. You can see this in the A1 answer list, e.g. matis for a word where an r is missing after the a.

Step 2 (A1): match each Latin word to an abbreviation

Sound out each option using the values above and see which Latin word it produces:

  • 1. fotis → f-o-(r missing)-tis = fortis, so (b) = 1.
  • 2. ītoductū → in-t-ro-ductum = introductum, so (f) = 2.
  • 3. 9u9sao → con-v-er-sa-(ti missing)-o = conversatio, so (a) = 3. Notice this also tells us the baseline sign 9 = con/com.
  • 4. 9pxio → com-p-(le missing)-x-io = complexio, so (c) = 4.
  • 5. cau97 → c-a-v-er-et = caveret, so (e) = 5.
  • 6. matis → ma-(r missing)-tis = martis, so (d) = 6.

Step 3 (A2): spot the odd one out

Expand all five: 9probatum = comprobatum; cōprobatū = com-probatu(m) = comprobatum; compobatum = comp-ro-batum = comprobatum; 9probatū = comprobatum. But 9probat9 ends in the word-final “us” sign, giving comprobatus — a different word. Answer: d.

Step 4 (A3): the ampersand

& comes from e + t and means “et”. We already discovered from p7 = pet that 7 stands for et (this is the real historical “Tironian et”). Answer: a.

Step 5 (A4): the symbol-bank jigsaw

Now look at what the bank does not contain: there is no plain r, no plain m, and no plain u. So wherever a word needs those letters, you must use a shortcut sign. Working each word:

  • (a) procatis: no plain r, so start with ꝑ (pro) = 17, then c a t i s = 2 1 14 6 13. → 17 2 1 14 6 13
  • (b) notarum: n o t a = 9 10 14 1, then the “rum” sign = 18. → 9 10 14 1 18
  • (c) decernimus: d e c = 3 4 2, then er = 22, n = 9, im (i with bar) = 7, and final us = 22. This uses both copies of 22. → 3 4 2 22 9 7 22
  • (d) congnitio: con = 21, g = 5, n = 9, i = 6, then a superscript o (11) with the t left out: congni(t)o. → 21 5 9 6 11
  • (e) crux: there is no plain r and no plain u, only superscript u (15). So c + u + x = 2 15 16. → 2 15 16
  • (f) petitur: the final ur must be 19. For “pet” you might be tempted to write p-e-t, but the bank contains a 7 (“et”) that has to be used somewhere, and petitur is the only word here containing “et”. So p + 7 + i + 2 = 12 20 6 19. → 12 20 6 19

Checking the counts confirms nothing is over-used: 22 is used exactly twice, 9 three times (out of four), 2 three times (out of four), and so on.

Step 6 (A5): the leftovers

Cross off every number you used. What remains is one a (1), one c (2), one d (3), one e (4), the l (8) and one n (9). Rearranged: candle — exactly what a monk squinting at a manuscript in a dim scriptorium would want for his birthday.

Answer keys taken from the official NACLO 2024 Round 1 solutions (A1: a3 b1 c4 d6 e5 f2; A2 D; A3 A; A4 as listed; A5 candle). Points per part are my even distribution (NACLO does not publish the breakdown): A1 6×0.5, A2 1, A3 1, A4 6×0.5, A5 2 = 10.

GLYPH APPROXIMATIONS: the 'pro' sign (bank #17) is typed in the PDF as a p with a crossed descender; I used U+A751 ꝑ. The 'rum' sign (bank #18) is a crossed r-rotunda (looks like a 2 with a slash); I used U+A75D ꝝ. Symbols 19-22 are typed in the PDF exactly as superscript 2, baseline 7, baseline 9, superscript 9 and are transcribed that way. The macron over 'uu' in īp⁹p7ūū spans BOTH u's in the original; rendered here with a text-decoration:overline span. Single-letter macrons use ī / ō / ū.

The SYMBOL BANK in the PDF is laid out as boxes of symbol-over-number with duplicates shown individually; I reorganized it into a Number / Symbol / Copies table (same information). Reviewer may wish to confirm the copy counts against the image: a×3, c×4, d×2, e×2, g×1, i×3, ī×1, l×1, n×4, o×1, superscript-o×1, p×1, s×1, t×2, superscript-u×1, x×1, ꝑ×1, ꝝ×1, superscript-2×1, 7×1, 9×1, superscript-9×2 (leftovers must spell 'candle').
